coredata.dc:description: The development of a superb polyethylene terephthalate (PET) hydrolyzing enzyme requires an accurate understanding of the PET decomposition mechanism. However, studies on PET degrading enzymes, including the PET hydrolase from Ideonella sakaiensis (IsPETase), have not provided sufficient knowledge of the molecular mechanisms for the hardly accessible substrate. Here, we report a novel PET hydrolase from Rhizobacter gummiphilus (RgPETase), which has a hydrolyzing activity similar to IsPETase toward microcrystalline PET but distinct behavior toward low crystallinity PET film. Structural analysis of RgPETase reveals that the enzyme shares the key structural features of IsPETase for high PET hydrolysis activity but has distinguished structures at the surface-exposed regions. RgPETase shows a unique conformation of the wobbling tryptophan containing loop (WW-loop) and change of the electrostatic surface charge on the loop dramatically affects the PET-degrading activity. We further show that effect of the electrostatic surface charge to the activity varies depending on locations. This work provides valuable information underlying the uncovered PET decomposition mechanism.

ce:abstract-sec.ce:simple-para: The development of a superb polyethylene terephthalate (PET) hydrolyzing enzyme requires an accurate understanding of the PET decomposition mechanism. However, studies on PET degrading enzymes, including the PET hydrolase from Ideonella sakaiensis (IsPETase), have not provided sufficient knowledge of the molecular mechanisms for the hardly accessible substrate. Here, we report a novel PET hydrolase from Rhizobacter gummiphilus (RgPETase), which has a hydrolyzing activity similar to IsPETase toward microcrystalline PET but distinct behavior toward low crystallinity PET film. Structural analysis of RgPETase reveals that the enzyme shares the key structural features of IsPETase for high PET hydrolysis activity but has distinguished structures at the surface-exposed regions. RgPETase shows a unique conformation of the wobbling tryptophan containing loop (WW-loop) and change of the electrostatic surface charge on the loop dramatically affects the PET-degrading activity. We further show that effect of the electrostatic surface charge to the activity varies depending on locations. This work provides valuable information underlying the uncovered PET decomposition mechanism.

ce:section.ce:para: Plastics are one of the best inventions of the 20th century and has become essential in human lives due to their desirable properties. However, as the most of plastics are non-degradable, plastic wastes are accumulated in landfills and ocean, resulting in serious environmental problems (Barnes et al., 2009). Polyethylene terephthalate (PET) is widely utilized plastic as packaging, container, and fiber and is produced by polymerization of ethylene glycol (EG) and terephthalate (TPA). Due to the ester bond of PET, various microbial hydrolases including cutinases (Müller et al., 2005; Ronkvist et al., 2009; Heumann et al., 2006; Sulaiman et al., 2012; Kawai et al., 2014; Roth et al., 2014), lipases (Eberl et al., 2009; de Castro and Carniel, 2017), and carboxylesterases (Ribitsch et al., 2011; Oeser et al., 2010) have been reported to degrade the unnatural polyester. The enzymatic degradation has a special role in monomer recovery of plastics, because the specificity of the enzyme allows selective degradation of plastics (Mueller, 2006; Tournier et al., 2020).

Moreover, microbes carrying the PET-degrading hydrolases can deal with the waste in the environment, and the cells can be utilized as a “one-pot” process to valorize the monomer recycling (Koshti et al., 2018; Hiraga et al., 2019; Kumari and Chaudhary, 2020). The concept of circular economy of PET is thought to be facilitated by the PET-degrading hydrolases and microorganisms secreting these enzymes. In this circumstance, isolation of Ideonella sakaiensis utilizing PET as a carbon source received a spotlight in this research field (Yoshida et al., 2016a,b; Tanasupawat et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2016). The mesophilic bacterium has a polyester endo-hydrolase named as PET hydrolase (IsPETase) as well as the mono(2-hydroxyethyl) terephthalate (MHET) hydrolase (IsMHETase) (Yoshida et al., 2016a). Most of environmental PET wastes are placed under ambient temperature (0–40 °C), and the hydrophobic substrate become more inert material at the conditions (Chamas et al., 2020; Furukawa et al., 2019). IsPETase exhibited much higher activities toward PET than other known hydrolases under ambient temperature (Yoshida et al. 2016a). Extensive structural studies on IsPETase have also been performed to explain its superb PET degradation ability and suggested its unique characteristics, such as the wobbling tryptophan (Han et al., 2017), high flexibility of the active site (Fecker et al., 2018), and the active site plateau with the additional disulfide bond and the extended loop (Joo et al., 2018; Austin et al., 2018). Furthermore, various IsPETase variants with much higher thermal stability and several expression and secretion systems for IsPETase in unnatural hosts were reported (Son et al., 2019, 2020; Cui et al., 2021; Seo et al., 2019; Huang et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2020; Moog et al., 2019).

Although intensive studies have been carried out within a few years, the strategies of IsPETase and microscopic mechanism of enzymatic PET degradation are still not clear. Enzymes with distinguished features to IsPETase but highly homologous to that, can specify the key mechanism of PET hydrolase toward PET at the ambient temperature. Our research group previously classified the 69 cutinase-like sequences into type I, IIa, and IIb, and the type IIb hydrolases possess most of the key structural features of IsPETase (Joo et al., 2018). However, we found local de-aligned regions of IsPETase with the amino acid sequence of A4W93_RS06010 from Rhizobacter gummiphilus NS21 (72% identity to IsPETase), one of the type IIb hydrolases. The regions include the residue Ser214 of IsPETase, predicted to make space for wobbling of the tryptophan (Han et al., 2017), and A4W93_RS06010 has His211 residue at the position. We thus focused on enzymatic activities of A4W93_RS06010, hoping that the characteristics can elucidate common sense of enzymatic degradation of the hardly accessible substrate. In this study, we report that A4W93_RS06010 from Rhizobacter gummiphilus is a novel PET hydrolase, with comparable hydrolysis activities to IsPETase against microcrystalline PET. Based on structural and mutational studies on the protein, we provide implications for the key structural features and surface electrostatic charge to PET-degrading activity of PETase.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Identification of a novel PET hydrolase
ce:section.ce:para:
To examine PET degradation ability of A4W93_RS06010, we first expressed the protein using the pET-21a system and obtained a purified protein with low yield ( Fig. 1A and Tables S1, S2). To increase protein folding, we then performed periplasmic secretory expression, because A4W93_RS06010 was predicted to have an additional disulfide bond as IsPETase that prefers the oxidizing condition for proper folding. Among six signal peptides, such as DsbA, PelB, LamB, SurA, MalE, and TolB (Seo et al., 2019), we tested (Table S2), we observed increased soluble expression of periplasmic A4W93_RS06010 from the signal peptides of PelB, LamB, or MalE, and the highest amount of the protein was obtained via the MalE system with 4-fold higher soluble expression than the cytoplasmic system (Fig. 1A). Both the purified cytoplasmic and periplasmic A4W93_RS06010 proteins eluted as a monomer in size-exclusion chromatography (Fig. S1) and had melting temperature (T
m ) of 48.5 °C, which is slightly lower than that of IsPETase (Son et al., 2019) (Fig. S2). The kcat and km values of cytoplasmic A4W93_RS06010 for bis(2-hydroxyethyl) terephthalate (BHET) were 28.5 s−1 and 148.8 nM, respectively, and those of periplasmic protein showed quite similar values with 30.1 s−1 and 151.6 nM, respectively (Fig. 1B).

To validate the PET-degrading activity of A4W93_RS06010, we measured the hydrolysis activities of the protein toward microcrystalline PET (mc-PET, Fig. S10) at the ambient temperatures such as 30 °C and 40 °C and compared with those of IsPETase. A4W93_RS06010 hydrolyzed mc-PET into MHET and terephthalate (TPA), and the activities were almost identical to IsPETase at these temperatures (Figs. 1C, and S3), suggesting that the type IIb hydrolase A4W93_RS06010 is a PET hydrolase. The activities were not maintained even for 1 day at 40 °C in both A4W93_RS06010 and IsPETase, whereupon the activities at 30 °C were totally higher than at 40 °C (Fig. 1C). Hereinafter, we designate A4W93_RS06010 as RgPETase, and to our knowledge, this is the first PET hydrolase that has a similar level of PET-degrading activity to IsPETase at the ambient temperatures. Next, we measured the hydrolysis activities of RgPETase and IsPETase toward low crystallinity PET film (lcPET, Goodfellow Ind, Fig. S10) and observed significantly lower activities with RgPETase compared to IsPETase (Figs. 1D, and S3). The results suggest that two highly homologous PET hydrolases can have an erratic relationship of activities against different PET samples.

In order to identify key structural region for PET-degrading activity of RgPETase, we determined its crystal structure at a 2.3 Å resolution (Fig. S4 and Table S4). RgPETase shows a quite similar structure to IsPETase with an alpha-carbon root mean square deviation of 0.291 Å and shares key structural features of IsPETase for high PET-hydrolyzing activity at the active site (Han et al., 2017; Fecker et al., 2018; Joo et al., 2018; Austin et al., 2018; Chen et al., 2018); the residues constituting the catalytic triad, the substrate binding site, the extended β8-α6 connecting loop, and the two disulfide bonds in IsPETase are almost identical and/or highly conserved in RgPETase ( Figs. 2A, B, S5, and S6). Thus, the high activities of RgPETase toward mc-PET at 30 °C seem to be derived from these structural characteristics.

However, we observed substantial structural differences between these two enzymes, especially in the surface-exposed areas (Fig. 2A, B). First, the variable region 1 (VR1, Q26-S51) is on the N-terminal loop and the α1-helix, and RgPETase and IsPETase shows 65.4% amino acid identity in the region (Fig. 2C). Second, the wobbling tryptophan containing loop (WW-loop, W183-S187) of RgPETase consists of distinct amino acids with five-residue cassette instead of six residues in IsPETase (W185-N190), resulting in noticeable structural differences between the two enzymes (Fig. 2D). Third, the variable region 2 (VR2, P207-V228) is on the α5-β7 region and contains His211 at the corresponding position of Ser214 in IsPETase. (Fig. 2E). Forth, the C-terminal region (G271-Y292) has almost no conserved residues and the additional amino acids of RgPETase form an extra α-helix (α8) (Fig. 2F). It is worthy to note that WW-loop, VR2, and C-terminal region form surface-exposed areas and are located in the vicinity of the active site plateau (Fig. 2A), and we speculate that these regions might affect the different behaviors of RgPETase and IsPETase toward lcPET.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Effect of WW-loop on PET-degrading activity
ce:section.ce:para: As we described, RgPETase shows a different conformation of WW-loop compared with IsPETase (Figs. 2D, and S7). WW-loop of RgPETase is unique even compared with other known PET hydrolases, such as cutinases from Thermobifida fusca KW3 (TfCut2), leaf-branch compost metagenome (LCC), Saccharomonospora viridis (Cut190), and Thermobifida cellulosilytica (Thc_Cut) ( Figs. 3A, and S6). We observed that the conformation of WW-loop is maintained by interactions between the loop and its neighboring regions including VR2 (Fig. 3B). Considering that the wobbling tryptophan mechanism in IsPETase has been suggested based on its unique Ser214 residue (Han et al., 2017), the networking seems to be related to PET-degrading activity. WW-loop of RgPETase is mainly stabilized by the Van der Waals forces with Phe215 and the hydrogen bonds with His211 and Gln218 (Fig. 3B). Moreover, a salt-bridge between Lys169 and Glu186 of WW-loop also restricts the loop to its positioning (Fig. 3B).

To verify the effect of these neighboring regions on the conformation of WW-loop, we replaced the His211, Phe215, and Gln218 residues with the residues of IsPETase and measured the PET-degrading activities of variants towards mc-PET at 30 °C. The RgPETaseF215I and RgPETaseQ218S variants showed reduced activity, and the RgPETaseH211S variant lost its activity more than 95% (Fig. 3C). These results indicated that the hydrogen bond between the main-chain sp2 nitrogen of A184 and Nδ of τ-tautomer H211 modulates the positioning of Trp183 in WW-loop and brings a drastic effect on the PET-degrading activity of RgPETase (Fig. 3B). We also produced the RgPETaseK169A, RgPETaseE186A, and RgPETaseK169A/E186A variants to abolish the salt bridge between Lys169 and Glu186, and all three variants showed decreased T
m (Fig. S8). The PET-degrading activities of RgPETaseE186A and RgPETaseK169A/E186A variants were decreased by 75% and 63%, respectively (Fig. 3C). Surprisingly, however, the RgPETaseK169A variant showed an enhanced activity compared to RgPETaseWT (Fig. 3C). Considering the decreased T
m value, the increased activity of the RgPETaseK169A variant has more important implications in terms of enzyme catalysis. This conflicting result cannot be explained by the elimination of the charge-charge interaction alone. To explain the phenomenon, we determined the crystal structures of the RgPETaseK169A and RgPETaseE186A variants (Fig. S9 and Table S4). Although we observed increased flexibility of WW-loop due to the mutation, the conformation of the loop is still maintained (Fig. 3D–F). However, the mutation caused a remarkable change of the electrostatic charge on the surface area. While the electrostatic charge of the two residues was neutralized by the salt bridge formation in RgPETaseWT (Fig. 3D), the original charge of one residue seems to be displayed due to the mutation of its counterpart residue (Fig. 3E, F). Based on these results, we suggest that the electrostatic charge of the WW-loop surface of RgPETase affects PET-hydrolyzing activity.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Effect of surface charge to PET-degrading activity
ce:section.ce:para: It was reported that increase of surface hydrophobicity in depolymerases promotes absorption process of the enzymes onto the polymer surface, and the rationale has been applied to PET degradation (Ribitsch et al., 2013, 2015; Biundo et al., 2018). However, our mutational study revealed that the negatively charged surface on WW-loop is advantageous to PET degradation and suggests that the electrostatic charge on surface of RgPETase might modulate the PET-degrading activity of the protein, without changing conformational states. The charge effect is also implied in the work showing that anionic surfactants accelerate PET degradation (Furukawa et al., 2018). Thus, we analyzed surface-exposed residues of RgPETase and selected six positively-charged residues, such as Arg45, Arg57, Arg88, Arg130, Arg221, and Arg281 ( Fig. 4A). We then replaced each of these residues to alanine or glutamate and measured their PET hydrolase activities toward mc-PET at 30 °C. Interestingly, the mutations of the arginine residues located distal from the active site plateau, such as Arg45, Arg57, Arg130, and Arg221, showed increased enzyme activity compared to RgPETaseWT (Fig. 4B). Especially, the RgPETaseR130A and RgPETaseR130E variants exhibited 1.6- and 1.7-fold increased activities in 1 day compared to RgPETaseWT (Fig. 4B). More interestingly, the enzyme activities of the Glu-substituted variants were slightly higher than those of the Ala-substituted variants (Fig. 4B). Taken together, the phenomenon is consistent to the results observed in the RgPETaseK169A variant, and we speculate that negative charge is more favorable than the positive charge on the surface area of RgPETase for PET-hydrolyzing activity.

However, the mutations of the positively-charged residues located in the vicinity of the active site plateau, such as Arg88 and Arg281, showed totally different results (Fig. 4B). The RgPETaseR88A and RgPETaseR88E variants showed significant decrease of activities by 24% and 28%, respectively, compared to RgPETaseWT (Fig. 4B). As the Arg88 residue is directly involved in the formation of the active site plateau, we speculated that neither hydrophobic nor negatively-charged surfaces are suitable for the accessibility of the PET substrate. On the other hand, the RgPETaseR281A and RgPETaseR281E variants exhibited the 1.9- and 1.5-fold enhanced activities in comparison to RgPETaseWT (Fig. 4B). These results indicated that residues adjacent to the active site plateau must have an optimal surface charge for efficient PET-degradation. Taken together, we conclude that the electrostatic surface charge of PET hydrolase plays an important role in the PET decomposition and the optimal conditions are totally different from region by region.

In this report, we present a novel PET-degrading enzyme, Rg PETase, which exhibits a PET-hydrolyzing activity similar to IsPETase under the ambient temperatures. The structural study of Rg PETase revealed that the enzyme shares the key structural features of IsPETase and supported that the key structural features for high PET-hydrolyzing activity suggested in IsPETase are also applied in Rg PETase. However, Rg PETase showed quite different PET-hydrolyzing activities toward two different PET samples, mc-PET and lcPET, compared with IsPETase. The results might have a significant impact to the research community noting that activities on PET film, powder, or model compounds do not correlate each other and screening PET hydrolase in a single substrate may be somewhat risky. In addition, although it is generally known that the enzyme more intensively degrades the amorphous region than the crystalline region of PET (Ronkvist et al., 2010), two PET hydrolases showed higher activities against mc-PET (17% crystallinity) than lcPET (6% crystallinity). We suspect that the increased surface area of mc-PET facilitated the accessibility and adsorption of the enzymes to the PET substrate. Our study cannot explain the lower PET-degrading activity of RgPETase toward lcPET compared to IsPETase, which indicates that an unidentified mechanism of IsPETase has been concealed in the structural differences between these two enzymes. Importantly, RgPETase exhibits a unique conformation of WW-loop, which is tightly regulated by residues such as His211. In addition, we showed that an electrostatic surface charge in several regions are important to the absorption process, and charge suitability to surface of PET hydrolase depends on region by region. This might be related to non-specific binding of the enzyme onto the PET surface. Taken together, this work presents a novel platform enzyme for investigation of uncovered mechanistic aspects of PET degradation and systematic development of superb PET-hydrolyzing variants.
